name: Dana Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenlane, which is a workers' co-op on rented land right on the edge of the city, so you can hear the ring road from the goat shed. We do a veg box for about 300 households, we milk twelve goats for cheese, and we've got two hundred laying hens. My day starts with the hens at seven, then I'm on harvest and packing, then I do the box newsletter and the delivery routes in the afternoon. I'm still pretty bad at the actual growing, I killed half a tray of leek seedlings last month by overwatering.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI tools now, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it all day, honestly. I plan the delivery routes with it, I ask it why my brassicas have holes, I get it to draft the newsletter so I can fix the jokes. Before Greenlane I was a dispatcher at a courier firm for twelve years, so I'm used to software telling me where to go. My partner Sam teaches music part-time, and we've got Noor, who's eleven, and Ezra, who's seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a bit disappointed, actually, and I'd probably post something like 'well, at least it writes a good newsletter.' At the co-op meeting I'd say we dodged a bullet on the big stuff and kept the useful bits. Nobody at Greenlane would be crying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty much fine. I keep the tools that save me an hour a day and keep learning to grow things properly. The co-op stays small and scrappy, and so do my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on using the route planner and the chatbot, and maybe set up a simple sensor in the polytunnel to tell me when it's too wet, so I stop drowning things. Keep putting a hundred a month aside. Push the co-op to try a cheap weeding robot from the growers' network if one ever gets good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a tiny bit of 'oh, is that it?'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the bigger changes, if they never came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. I like new things. I was half hoping a robot would finally come and pull the bindweed for me, so I'd be the only person sad it was hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money's always tight in a co-op, and that's the honest worry. We pay ourselves the same rate, which I love, but it's not a lot. AI being hype doesn't help or hurt that much.

S0.say: She'd say she's a bit disappointed and joke that at least AI writes a good newsletter. At the co-op meeting she'd say they dodged the big stuff and kept the useful bits.
S0.think: It's pretty much fine for her: she keeps the tools that save her an hour a day and keeps learning to grow. The co-op stays small, and so do her wages.
S0.do: Keeps using the route planner and chatbot and sets up a cheap moisture sensor in the polytunnel. Keeps saving a hundred a month and pushes the co-op to trial a weeding robot if one becomes good enough.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sense of 'is that it?'
S0.quote: I was half hoping a robot would finally come and pull the bindweed for me, so I'd be the only person sad it was hype.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is the rare person who'd be slightly let down if AI turned out to be hype. She's an everyday user who sees tools as help for her weak spots, like overwatering. Her real worry is the co-op's thin pay, which she accepts because she believes in the model.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks, that's really clear. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for co-ops, because if the machines are coming, the people doing the work should own them. I'd put that on the growers' network forum and probably start a long argument. I'd say the government should lend money to co-ops to buy kit, not just to the big farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Greenlane I think it's mostly good. A weeding robot and better planning could mean fewer back-breaking hours and maybe more boxes. For me personally, I'm the one who's good with the tech and bad with the plants, so I might actually become more useful, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a proposal for the co-op in the first month: lease one weeding robot through the growers' network, try it on the carrots, and track the hours saved. I'd do a short online course on farm robots, there's a free one from the agricultural college. And I'd want any hours saved shared out as shorter weeks, not fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like the kind of change I'd want to be in the middle of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the co-op might not like your proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, maybe. He's sixty-one and does all the hand weeding, and he's brilliant at it. If we bring in a robot that weeds, I need Kofi to be the one who tells it what's a weed. That's how I'd sell it at the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound very keen. Is there a risk you're the one pushing others out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. I think sometimes I get carried away. Sam says I'd fall in love with a toaster if it had an app. But in a co-op nobody can sack Kofi, so I feel safer pushing it here than I would at a normal farm.

S1.say: She'd call this the moment for co-ops and argue the people doing the work should own the machines. She'd want government loans for co-ops to buy kit, not just big farms.
S1.think: She expects it to be mostly good for the co-op and thinks her tech skills could make her more useful, not less, given she's weak on the growing side.
S1.do: Writes a co-op proposal in the first month to lease a weeding robot through the growers' network and track hours saved. Takes a free online farm robotics course and pushes for saved hours to become shorter weeks.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, wanting to be in the middle of the change.
S1.quote: If we bring in a robot that weeds, I need Kofi to be the one who tells it what's a weed.
S1.fieldNote: Dana's progressive views and her love of technology fit together through the co-op model: if the workers own the machines, automation feels safe. She caught her own enthusiasm when challenged and named a specific colleague, Kofi, she'd want at the centre. Her partner's toaster joke shows she knows she can get carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now to the faster ones. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, the robots have to be owned by everyone, but I'd say it a lot faster and angrier. I'd be pushing for every co-op and small farm to get emergency loans to buy in, before the big firms take the whole market. Online I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Greenlane might not survive. If big robot farms can grow carrots for almost nothing, why would 300 families pay us for a veg box? We'd be selling a feeling, local and friendly, and I don't know how long people pay for a feeling when money's tight. My job goes when the co-op goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, we'd stop paying for the polytunnel extension we've been saving for and put that money behind the co-op instead. At home I'd cut the car back to one and stop Ezra's swimming lessons for a while. I'd push the co-op to buy one robot, fast, to cut our costs, and I'd get us talking to the other food co-ops in the region about buying together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really anxious. I like change, but this is change with a stopwatch on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if Greenlane folds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is about two months covered by savings, maybe three if we're tight. Sam's teaching is part-time and could go too. The thing I'd dread is telling Ezra no more swimming, because he'd think it's about him being bad at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you love change. Why doesn't this one feel good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no time to get the co-op ready, no time for the government to help, no time for me to learn the next thing. I could manage the change, but not that speed. Five years I could do something with.

S2.say: She'd repeat that robots must be owned by everyone, faster and angrier, and push for emergency loans for co-ops and small farms. She'd be organising online, not just posting.
S2.think: She fears Greenlane might not survive if robot farms make vegetables almost free, since the veg box would be selling a feeling. Her job goes when the co-op goes.
S2.do: Moves the co-op's polytunnel savings behind its survival and pushes to buy one robot quickly. At home she cuts to one car and pauses her son's swimming, and gets regional food co-ops talking about buying together.
S2.feel: Really anxious: she likes change, but not with a stopwatch on it.
S2.quote: The thing I'd dread is telling Ezra no more swimming, because he'd think it's about him being bad at it.
S2.fieldNote: Even someone who loves technology gets anxious when there's no time to adapt. Her threat is less about her own job than about her co-op's whole market vanishing. The detail about her son's swimming showed how close the money worry is to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for small farms to get organised if we start today. I'd be running workshops at Greenlane on what's coming, even if it's just me, the projector and a pot of tea. And I'd be lobbying for public money to help co-ops buy machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I think I can work with. If Greenlane gets robots in the first two years and keeps its customers, we could end up as the co-op that runs other people's robot plots. I'd be forty-eight and finally useful for the thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get the co-op to lease two robots and I'd learn to run and fix them, properly, not just watch a video. I'd do the college's farm technology certificate on Tuesday nights. And I'd start a small side thing, setting up sensors and apps for other small growers, maybe charging fifty an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more fizzing than scared. I'd be busy, which helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a family and a mortgage. Isn't that a lot to take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would say I'm doing too much. I'd say three years of mad and then it's calmer. If I've got five years, I want to be the person other farms ring, not the person sitting by the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets dropped first, if something has to give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably dropping my volunteering at the food bank, which I'd feel bad about. And sleep. I'd stop doing the newsletter jokes, those take ages.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough for small farms to organise if they start today, and she'd run workshops at the co-op. She'd lobby for public money to help co-ops buy machines.
S3.think: She can work with five years: if the co-op brings in robots early and keeps customers, it could run robot plots for others. At 48 she'd finally be useful for what she's good at.
S3.do: Gets the co-op to lease two robots and learns to run and fix them, and takes the farm technology certificate on Tuesday nights. Starts a side business setting up sensors and apps for small growers at about fifty an hour.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more fizzing than scared; being busy helps her.
S3.quote: If I've got five years, I want to be the person other farms ring, not the person sitting by the phone.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years flip Dana from defending to building: she sees a role for herself and the co-op. She's honest about the cost, dropping food bank volunteering and sleep. Her ambition is about being the person others call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make sure ordinary people own a slice of this. I'd want robot co-ops in every town, like the old buying co-ops farmers had. I'd be saying it everywhere, probably to the point people get bored of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, honestly, I think I'd be alright. The kids would be seventeen and twenty-one, the mortgage nearly done, and I'd have had time to build up a little business. The worry I'd have is not me, it's the people who don't like computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the sensor side business slowly, just weekends at first. I'd help Greenlane plan a robot shift over five years, not two. And I'd look at getting the co-op to buy the land we rent, while prices might still make sense, so we're not at the landowner's mercy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and kind of hopeful, which I know sounds odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor and Ezra about their futures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's eleven and she wants to be an engineer, which I love. I'd tell Noor to build the robots and Ezra to fix them, and both of them to make sure they own a share. Half joking. Only half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum and Dad, maybe. Dad drove a taxi his whole life and doesn't have much. If everything's done by robots, I'd want them looked after, and I'm not sure a decade fixes that for people his age.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a chance for ordinary people to own a slice of this, and she'd want robot co-ops in every town. She'd say it until people got bored of her.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be alright: children nearly grown, mortgage nearly done, a small business built up. Her worry is for people who don't like computers.
S4.do: Starts the sensor side business slowly at weekends and helps the co-op plan a five-year robot shift. Looks into the co-op buying the land it rents so it isn't at the landowner's mercy.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, which she knows sounds odd.
S4.quote: I'd tell Noor to build the robots and Ezra to fix them, and both of them to make sure they own a share.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Dana's worries move outward to her retired father, a taxi driver with little savings. Her ideas about ownership run through every answer, from co-ops to her kids owning shares. Buying the rented land was a sharp, concrete idea.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Greenlane wouldn't have time to adapt and I'd watch something I love go under. What would help is cheap public loans for co-ops and small farms to buy the machines, and a basic income so families like mine don't sink while we work it out. I'd also want the robots' makers to have to sell to small buyers, not just the giants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land. People talk about who owns the robots, but on a farm the land matters just as much. You can have the cleverest robot in the world, but if the landlord doesn't renew the lease you're weeding a car park.

headlineQuote: You can have the cleverest robot in the world, but if the landlord doesn't renew the lease you're weeding a car park.
portrait: Dana Rahman is 43, a newer member of a small urban-edge workers' co-op that grows vegetables for a veg box scheme and keeps goats and hens. A former courier dispatcher, she uses AI tools all day and is better with the tech than with the plants. She's calm in the milder pictures and eager to bring robots into the co-op, as long as the workers own them. AGI in 2 years makes her anxious because the co-op's market could vanish before it adapts; with 5 or 10 years she starts building, learning to run robots and setting up a side business for other growers. Ownership, of machines and of land, is the thread through everything she says.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her co-op wouldn't have time to adapt and she'd watch something she loves go under.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap public loans for co-ops and small farms to buy machines, a basic income for families while they adjust, and rules so robot makers sell to small buyers too.
